overview: SEGRO is a UK-listed Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) that owns, manages and develops modern industrial and logistics property across the UK and seven other European countries, with a ~10.9 million sq m (117 million sq ft) portfolio spanning urban warehouses, big box logistics parks and a growing data centre platform (c.8% of portfolio value). The company is currently the subject of a recommended £14bn+ all-share-plus-cash takeover by US logistics REIT Prologis, approved by SEGRO shareholders on 28 September 2026 and now awaiting court sanction and regulatory clearances, with completion targeted for H1 2027 — this corporate action is the dominant near-term driver of the investment case.

business_model.summary: SEGRO earns recurring rental income from long-let industrial, logistics and data centre real estate, supplemented by development profits from converting its land bank into income-producing assets and selective capital recycling (disposals above book value funding new investment). Revenue is overwhelmingly recurring contracted rent with annual/index-linked uplifts and periodic rent reviews capturing reversion (mark-to-market gap between passing and market rent).
business_model.customer_type: B2B — diverse base of 1,371+ businesses across 35+ sectors (transport & logistics 25%, retail 18%, food/general manufacturing 15%, post & parcel 10%, wholesale distribution 9%, data centre operators 7%); tenants include Amazon, DHL, Royal Mail, GXO, FedEx, Iron Mountain, Equinix, Virtus
business_model.geographic_mix: UK 62%, Germany 12%, France 11%, Italy 6%, Poland 4%, Netherlands 2%, Spain 2%, Czech Republic 1% (by portfolio value, SEGRO share)

competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest pan-European industrial/logistics REITs and the leading owner-operator of urban/infill warehousing in supply-constrained European cities, plus Europe's largest single data centre cluster (Slough Trading Estate). Being acquired by sector leader Prologis, which would create a combined group managing ~$269bn of assets.

moat_factors.description: £1.6bn land bank (c.8% of portfolio value) in supply-constrained urban locations with restrictive planning regimes limiting new competing supply
19 offices in 9 countries with deep local market knowledge, data-driven location assessments and long-standing customer relationships (26% of rent from multi-country customers)
2.5GW+ potential capacity pipeline, strategic power/grid connections secured years in advance — a genuine barrier to entry increasingly valued by hyperscalers
Modest leverage (31% LTV) but Prologis argues its own larger, more diversified capital base can unlock SEGRO's land bank faster than SEGRO could standalone

weaknesses: Persistent share price discount to EPRA NTA (925p NTA vs. trading meaningfully below that for periods pre-bid), cited by Prologis as a rationale for the opportunistic approach
UK portfolio has underperformed the MSCI benchmark (5.2% TPR vs 7.2% benchmark in 2025)
Older London assets (West London) requiring refurbishment/redevelopment create elevated vacancy drag in sub-markets
Development capex and yields are sensitive to construction cost inflation and financing rates
As an acquisition target, independent strategic execution (including data centre buildout) is now subordinated to deal completion and Prologis's integration plans

growth_drivers: Data centre strategy: 2.5GW+ potential capacity pipeline (0.5GW operational, generating £58m headline rent, 7% of rent roll), joint ventures with Pure Data Centres Group (two JVs signed) to deliver fully-fitted data centres capturing Cloud/AI-driven demand

Development pipeline: £441m of potential rent across current/near-term (£90m) and future (£223m owned land + £128m optioned land) pipeline at 7-8% yields; land bank (577 hectares, £1.6bn) able to support 2.6m sq m of development over 5-7 years
Reversion capture: portfolio 12% reversionary (c.£99m of further headline rent available), with record uplifts on UK rent reviews/renewals (+44% H1 2026, +36% FY2025)
UK big box JV: new 50:50 joint venture seeded with ~£1bn of SEGRO land/assets to accelerate big box logistics development with non-recourse partner funding
Disciplined capital recycling: selective disposals above book value (£308m in 2025/H1-2026 combined) funding reinvestment into higher-return development

If the Prologis deal completes: access to a larger, better-capitalised global platform (public and private capital) to accelerate monetisation of the land bank and data centre pipeline faster than SEGRO could alone

business.description: The Prologis combination, while shareholder-approved, remains subject to Court sanction and multiple regulatory approvals; failure or delay would leave SEGRO's share price exposed to downside given the deal underpins the current valuation
Industrial/logistics demand is tied to e-commerce, trade volumes and manufacturing activity; slower occupier decision-making already pushed back some 2025 development starts
Speculative development and data centre buildout carry leasing, cost-inflation and timing risk; grid connection delays could slow data centre monetisation
Rent lost to insolvency was low in 2025 (£4m, 0.5% of rent) but logistics/retail tenants are cyclical

financial.description: REIT valuations and NAV are sensitive to cap rate/yield movements; pro forma NAV already dipped slightly in H1 2026 (905p vs 925p FY2025) on valuer yield assumption changes
LTV rose to 31% in 2025 (from 28%) due to investment activity, though still within stated tolerance
c.38% of portfolio value outside the UK (EUR-denominated), and a Prologis deal consideration partly in USD-equivalent Prologis stock introduces GBP/USD translation risk for UK shareholders

regulatory.description: The Prologis deal requires UK CMA clearance, EU Commission merger clearance, Italian Golden Power approval and UK National Security and Investment Act clearance; regulators are expected to scrutinise localized warehouse market overlaps
Scheme of arrangement requires Court sanction following the already-passed Court/General Meeting votes (28 Sept 2026)

macro.description: Industrial/logistics yields and capital values are sensitive to the broader real estate investment cycle and interest-rate environment across SEGRO's 8 European markets
Securing sufficient grid capacity across European markets is an industry-wide bottleneck that could slow the data centre growth driver

execution.description: New CFO (Susanne Schroeter) appointed during FY2025, alongside a pending change of ultimate ownership/control if the Prologis deal completes

If completed, integrating SEGRO into Prologis's global platform carries standard M&A execution risk around synergy capture, data centre JV continuity, and retention of SEGRO's European teams/local relationships

macro_factors.industry_outlook: European industrial/logistics real estate remains supported by structural trends (e-commerce penetration, supply chain reconfiguration/nearshoring, urban infill scarcity, and surging power-constrained data centre demand), though the sector faced a de-rating in 2023-2024 on higher interest rates before stabilising; 2025-2026 saw improving occupier sentiment and record rent reviews/pre-lets
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — rental income is relatively defensive/contracted with long leases (7-8 years to expiry) and indexation, but capital values and development pipeline economics are cyclical and rate-sensitive
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High for capital values/NAV (cap rate compression/expansion) and development funding costs; moderate for income given fixed/indexed long leases
key_input_costs: Electricity/grid connection costs for data centre buildout

recent_developments.event: Offer period begins; Prologis makes initial approaches to SEGRO, which the SEGRO board rejects as undervaluing the company (reported value c.£12.6bn-£13.5bn, c.993p-1,000p/share range)

Prologis submits 'Best and Final' proposal valuing SEGRO at ~£14bn: 0.0920 new Prologis shares per SEGRO share plus a partial cash alternative (up to 25% of consideration, max ~£3.5bn) fixed at 1,031.7p/share, a ~39% premium to the undisturbed price; stated as final absent a competing bid

SEGRO board agrees to recommend the Prologis combination; firm offer announced, implying a combined group managing ~$269bn of assets; SEGRO shareholders expected to hold ~8.9% of the enlarged Prologis group
Scheme Document published for the Court Meeting and General Meeting

SEGRO shareholders approve the Scheme at the Court Meeting and General Meeting (requisite majorities voted in favour); deal remains subject to Court sanction and outstanding regulatory approvals (UK CMA, EU Commission, Italian Golden Power, UK NSIA); completion still targeted for H1 2027

H1 2026 results: adjusted EPS growth 6.6%, EPRA NTA per share down 2.5% in the half; £53m of new headline rent contracted, £26m development signings, 5.3% like-for-like NRI growth, continued data centre JV progress with Pure Data Centres Group

H1 2026 trading update: new headline rent £53m (vs £31m H1 2025), pro forma adjusted NAV 905p (down slightly from 925p at FY2025 year-end on valuer yield assumption changes), FY2026 development capex guidance narrowed to top of range £500-550m, EPRA cost ratio improved to <18%

items.notes: Narrowed to the top end of the previous range, reflecting a record pipeline of projects under construction/advanced negotiations (£90m potential rent, 75% pre-let)

items.target: At or above upper end of medium/long-term run rate of 1-2% of portfolio per annum
items.notes: Higher bar for capital recycling given higher interest rate environment; £308m of disposals completed/exchanged by H1 2026
Down from 19.8% at FY2025 year-end, reflecting cost discipline
Expected to remain in normal range; 2025 completions achieved 8.2% partly boosted by data centre mix

guidance.management_commentary: CEO David Sleath described 'a very encouraging start to the year, with strong occupier momentum' and a record development pipeline; management emphasised disciplined capital allocation, selective acquisitions only where returns exceed cost of capital, and continued build-out of the data centre platform. Guidance since August 2026 has been superseded in practical investment terms by the pending Prologis takeover — the SEGRO board's own standalone medium-term targets are no longer the primary driver of shareholder outcomes while the Scheme is pending.

bull_case: Clear, near-term catalyst: shareholders have already approved the Prologis scheme (28 Sept 2026) at a ~39% premium to the undisturbed price (1,031.7p cash-equivalent value), with the main remaining risk being regulatory/court timing rather than deal logic

Irreplaceable, supply-constrained European land bank and urban warehouse portfolio provide a long-duration growth runway (land bank alone could support £355m of future rent) independent of the deal outcome

Data centre platform (2.5GW+ pipeline, Europe's largest single data centre cluster at Slough) is a high-growth, structurally advantaged business line benefiting from AI/Cloud-driven power demand, validated by Prologis's own stated rationale for the deal
Strong operational momentum: record rent reviews/renewals uplifts (+44% UK H1 2026), improving occupancy, high customer retention and satisfaction, and disciplined balance sheet (31% LTV)

If the deal completes, shareholders gain exposure to a larger, globally diversified, better-capitalised Prologis platform (~$269bn combined AUM) that can accelerate monetisation of SEGRO's embedded value faster than SEGRO could standalone
bear_case: Deal completion risk: Court sanction and multiple regulatory clearances (UK CMA, EU Commission, Italian Golden Power, UK NSIA) remain outstanding with completion not expected until H1 2027 — any blocking action, extended review, or required remedies could delay value realisation or, in a tail scenario, derail the deal

Consideration is mostly Prologis stock (plus a capped, pro-rata-scaled cash alternative), so UK holders take on Prologis share price volatility and GBP/USD currency risk between now and completion, and the implied deal value will fluctuate with Prologis's share price

Opportunistic-bid narrative: SEGRO's own board initially rejected three lower proposals as undervaluing the company's land bank and data centre optionality, implying the agreed price may still understate long-run intrinsic value if a standalone scenario had been pursued

Standalone operational risks persist regardless of the deal: occupier decision-making has slowed (development capex pushed back in 2025), UK portfolio has underperformed its MSCI benchmark, and NAV has already ticked down in H1 2026 on valuer yield assumption changes

Post-completion integration risk for any residual minority/combined-entity exposure: synergy realisation, data centre JV continuity, and retention of SEGRO's European teams and customer relationships are unproven and typical of large cross-border REIT mergers
